newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE - Britain's Blunkett pilots Blair's education drive.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Britain's Blunkett pilots Blair's education drive.

text.p: As a boy at boarding school, David Blunkett grew to love books by reading under his bedclothes after the dormitory lights were switched off.
But there was no torchlight to give him away as he filled his imagination with pirates and soccer stars.
For Blunkett, Labour's new Education Secretary, is blind and braille was his gateway to learning during a childhood marred by tragedy and poverty.

Blunkett is not a product of the private boarding schools that produced a stream of cabinet ministers during the 18 years of Conservative rule that ended on May 1, but of a state institute for blind children.
He overcame his disability to become the left-wing leader of Sheffield city council in northern England before entering parliament in 1987.
A decade later, he is piloting new Prime Minister Tony Blair's plans to improve the plight of the poor and dispossessed through "education, education, education".

Blunkett has had to trim his philosophy to fit the "radical centrist" ideas of Blair but his basic ideals, founded on personal experience, remain unaltered and in tune with Blair's belief that self-improvement comes through better education.
"Total dedication to getting kids who currently get a lousy deal on to the ladder of opportunity," is his reason for being in politics, he says.
BLUNKETT'S BELIEFS BASED ON BITTER EXPERIENCE
His belief that Labour should strive to make a difference to the lives of those at the bottom of the economic ladder is based on his own bitter experience.

An only child, Blunkett was born blind 50 years ago next month because of "genetic incompatibilities". At 12, his father, foreman in a gas works, died a lingering death after falling into a vat of boiling water at work.

"It was brought home to me very severely indeed that the world was an extremely unfair place," Blunkett says. "My mum spent two years desperately trying to get some compensation, during which time we literally on occasions just had bread and dripping (lard) in the house."
Blunkett was rarely at home as he was sent to a boarding school for the blind aged just four. It made him the man he is now, but it didn't leave much time for childhood.

"Going to this boarding school was horrendously dislocating and emotionally unhelpful. You need your mum and dad, you need to be held," he once said. "You learn to be independent, perhaps too self-reliant, you build up an outer shell and, as I'm maturing, only now can I restore a sense of humour and be prepared to allow emotions to show."
To the outside world, Blunkett appears a genial character with his woolly beard, pleasant smile and bluff Yorkshire tones. But not many survive trying to block his path.
His teachers thought he should aim to be a piano tuner and he left school without qualifications. But, by studying at night school, Blunkett won a place at Sheffield University.
An active Labour member, he became a city councillor at 22 while still at college. He married a teacher, Ruth, a year later but, after 20 years and three boys, they divorced.
"Politics became a substitute for a contented marriage although I didn't recognise this until years later," he says.
He was council leader at 33 and won a place on Labour's ruling body, the National Executive, before becoming a member of parliament.
Once in parliament, he was appointed health spokesman in 1992, shortly after Labour's fourth successive election defeat and took over the education brief two years later.

Despite Blair's keen interest in education, Blunkett has not had an easy time. He had to hold his tongue about Blair's decision to send his eldest son Euan to a school outside local authority control while then health spokeswoman Harriet Harman's child entered a school which selected pupils on merit.
Blair's move was not strictly against Labour policy but was viewed with disfavour by left-wingers.
Harman's, however, directly opposed Labour policy on "selective" schools and was roundly condemned by many in the party. Blunkett was reported to be furious with his colleague.

In early 1995 he was roughed up by trade unionists at a teachers' conference in an incident that distressed many television viewers. But Blunkett said his blindness should not accord him special treatment and said he was deeply insulted when the unionists apologised because of his disability.
"My blindness is purely incidental. It just focuses on the fact I can't see, rather than the job I am doing."

In their 18 years in power, the Conservatives alienated teachers by introducing league tables showing the best and worst performers among schools and introducing a national curriculum and regular testing of young pupils.
EDUCATION TOP PRIORITY FOR NEW GOVERNMENT
During the election campaign, Blair targeted education as a top priority, reacting to public fears about falling standards and of a widening split between good and bad schools.
Labour plans two education bills -- one aimed at reducing classroom sizes to 30 pupils and the second to raise standards by increasing powers to remove poor teachers.
Blunkett says that, despite spending constraints, transforming education is an evangelical cause for him and his ministry has transformed its practices to accommodate him.

He will receive shorter submissions than normal and brailing equipment will be more readily available. Blunkett prefers to take in information from tapes and clear-voiced officials have been picked to record as much as possible.
